newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Dole spar in final campaign weekend.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Dole spar in final campaign weekend.

text.p: In the final weekend of the campaign, President Bill Clinton on Saturday accused Republicans of divisive politics but challenger Bob Dole continued to hammer at Clinton's ethics.

"We've had literally a scandal a week in this administration the past several weeks," Dole said in Indianapolis. "I think the American people are starting to say 'What's going on there. What's going on in this White House?'"
With just three days to go until Tuesday's election, Dole stayed with attacks on Clinton's ethics in the second day of the Republican's round-the-clock campaign push for the White House.
"If he's re-elected he's going to spend half of his time next year with investigations ... who knows what will happen in the next 24 months, 36 months," Dole said.
Clinton countered at a speech at the Alamo in San Antonio by accusing Republicans of divisive politics.

"Why is the election in doubt? Why aren't we ahead in Texas in the polls?" Clinton said. "It is because we have practiced the politics of division for so long. We have tried to turn our opponents into aliens."
Clinton made the campaign stop at the Alamo to try to win over normally Republican Texas despite a local poll showing he was trailing 47-42 in voter support there.
Dole narrowed Clinton's lead in the final days of the campaign, two voter opinion polls showed.

Picking up undecided voters, Dole narrowed Clinton's lead to 3.8 percent in a Reuters/Zogby daily tracking poll. Clinton was favoured by 42.4 percent and Dole 38.6 percent of 1,200 likely voters polled by John Zogby Group International between Wednesday and Friday. The poll had a three percentage point margin of error.

Dole also narrowed Clinton's lead in a CNN/USA Today Gallup poll, but more modestly. It showed a 13 percent Clinton lead Saturday, 50 percent to Dole's 37 percent, compared to an 18 point Clinton lead on Friday.

Reform Party candidate Ross Perot was far behind in third but White House officials hoped the third party candidate would not cut into Clinton's margin so much that the president would be denied a majority of the popular vote.

White House political director Doug Sosnick, travelling with Clinton in Texas, said undecided voters were finally making a choice in the final days before the election and he was not suprised that Clinton was getting few of them.
Dole said early in the day in his marathon 96-hour campaign that "we are going to win this election" and told reporters travelling with him that the vote was moving in his direction.
"I think it's tightening up everywhere," Dole said. "A lot of good numbers floating around. A lot of polls out tomorrow."
Dole started the day with a chat at an all-night coffee shop in New Jersey and went on to breakfast with retired Gen. Colin Powell outside of Philadelphia.
"It's a race ... that is winnable and he's going to win it," Powell, who was chairman of the military Joint Chiefs of Staff, told a crowd of several hundred at a restaurant along the Delaware River.
"We are going to win this election," Dole responded.
At the Alamo, Clinton compared himself to Texas heroes for standing up to Congress on the budget.

Addressing a large, friendly crowd at a rally at the shrine of Texas liberty, Clinton recalled his policy scrap with the Republicans late last year that twice shut the government, and said, "I thought about the Alamo."

"They said, "Oh, he'll blink.' And I said, 'You know, I'd a lot rather see the American people hurt for two or three weeks or two or three months than 20 or 30 years. Shut her down, I'm not going to buy your budget'," Clinton said.
